summary:
This is the opening page of **chapter 6, "The universal workflow of machine learning."**

**This chapter covers:**
- Framing a machine learning problem
- Developing a working model
- Deploying your model in production and maintaining it

The opening text points out that all previous examples assumed a labeled dataset already existed, so training could start immediately. In the real world, "you don't start from a dataset; you start from a problem."

To make this concrete, the authors ask you to imagine launching your own ML consulting shop. Projects start rolling in; the first two on this page are:
- a **personalized photo search engine** for a picture-sharing social network (type "wedding" and retrieve your wedding pictures with no manual tagging), and
- **flagging spam and offensive text** in the posts of a budding chat app.

The list continues on p.196 (music recommendation, credit card fraud, ad click-through rate, anomalous cookies on a production line, archaeological sites from satellite images), followed by the three-part structure of the workflow: define the task, develop a model, deploy the model.

**How to use this page:** treat the chapter map below as your roadmap; as you read each project, ask yourself what the input data, target, and success metric would be — that is exactly what section 6.1 teaches.

paragraphs.excerpt: Our previous examples have assumed that we already had a labeled dataset
paragraphs.what_it_says: Earlier examples assumed a labeled dataset was available so a model could be trained right away; in reality this is often not so. You start from a problem, not a dataset.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The hardest and most consequential work often happens before any model is trained: deciding what to predict, what data to collect, and how to label it.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It reframes ML engineering as problem solving, motivating sections 6.1.1–6.1.4 (framing, collecting data, understanding data, choosing a success measure).

terminology.meaning: Inputs paired with target answers, required for supervised learning.

paragraphs.excerpt: Imagine that you’re launching your own machine learning consulting shop. You
paragraphs.what_it_says: A scenario: you start an ML consulting business and receive projects. The first two are a personalized photo search engine that retrieves pictures by typed concepts like 'wedding' without manual tagging, and flagging spam and offensive text in a new chat app.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each request is phrased in business terms, not ML terms. Photo search implies image understanding (possibly classification or embedding images and text into a shared space); spam/offensive flagging implies text classification. Neither comes with a dataset.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: These examples are reused in section 6.1 to illustrate how to frame problems and collect data.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: 'without any manual tagging needed' refers to the end user; the developer may still need labeled data to train the system.
connections: p.196: the list of projects continues

concepts.name: Universal workflow of machine learning
concepts.definition: A step-by-step blueprint for approaching any ML problem: define the task, develop a model, deploy the model.
concepts.intuition: A checklist that takes you from a vague customer request to a maintained model in production.
concepts.technical: Covered in sections 6.1 (defining the task), 6.2 (developing a model) and 6.3 (deploying your model).
concepts.significance: Consolidates chapters 4 and 5 and anchors the rest of the book.
concepts.example: Turning 'flag spam in our chat app' into a text classifier with a measurable success metric.
concepts.misconception: That ML work begins with model training.

misconceptions.claim: Real ML projects start with a dataset ready to train on.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter opens by stressing that you start from a problem; the dataset usually has to be collected and labeled.

takeaways: Chapter 6 covers framing an ML problem, developing a working model, and deploying and maintaining it.
You don't start from a dataset; you start from a problem.
Real requests (photo search, spam/offensive content flagging) are phrased in business terms and arrive without data.
